soil-env-298.title: Itai-itai disease, the poisoned rice of the Jinzū River
soil-env-298.text: For 55 years, people along Japan's Jinzū River fell ill without knowing why. Itai-itai disease was a mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, beginning around 1912 and named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused. It is the best-known case of the illness in {{ref:soil-env-256}}. Mines upstream released cadmium into the river from 1910 to 1945. The metal travels with zinc, because the zinc ore sphalerite is almost always paired with greenockite. Residents irrigated their rice with the river water. The highly soluble cadmium soaked into paddies and grain, and body burdens rose. It built up in the kidneys, and damaged kidneys upset the body's calcium balance, bringing bone pain and deformities. Cadmium was suspected only in 1955. A 1961 investigation tied it to the Kamioka mine, 55 years after the first reports. It became one of the Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan, and the mining company was successfully sued.

soil-env-293.title: Valley fever, the illness that rides on dust
soil-env-293.text: In 1977 a windstorm near Arvin, California, caused several hundred cases of a lung disease hundreds of miles from where it normally occurs. The disease was coccidioidomycosis, or valley fever: a fungal disease of mammals caught by inhaling spores of the soil fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii. Like the fungi in {{ref:soil-bio-003}}, it grows as a web of threads, in soils of the southwestern US, northern Mexico and parts of Central and South America. Rain starts its growth. In long dry spells its threads, the hyphae, break into light spores called arthroconidia. Construction, farming, dust storms or earthquakes then lift them into the air. Cases rise after wet winters that follow drought, and one model projects the endemic region could more than double in area by 2100 under high warming. Planting grass and wetting soil keep the dust down. NIOSH counts it an occupational hazard in farming, construction, archaeology and mining. Dogs, which dig and sniff at the ground, are exposed earlier than people and serve as sentinels.

soil-env-287.title: Medical geology: when the ground decides who falls ill
soil-env-287.text: Hippocrates and Aristotle were the first to link disease to the elements of the earth. Medical geology is the modern form of that idea: the interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals. The International Union of Geological Sciences established the field in 1990. It covers exposure to, or deficiency of, trace elements and {{ref:soil-found-029}}, along with mineral dusts, volcanic emissions, radionuclides, microbes and pathogens. Two priorities lead the work. One is the bioavailability of trace elements, the share the body can actually absorb. The other is the baseline background level of harmful natural materials in soil, water, air and food. People who live off the land meet both extremes. In Maputaland, impoverished soils cause diseases of mineral imbalance. In India and Bangladesh, an excess of elements causes toxicity. A shortage of iodine is among the biggest geochemical diseases, partly because humus and clay in soil trap iodine and keep it from people. Other problems are regional: fluoride in Africa and India, arsenic in Argentina, Chile and Taiwan, selenium in parts of the US, Venezuela and China, and nitrate in farm areas. Paracelsus summed up the field in one dictum: the dose makes the poison. Its goal is the right balance of element intake.

soil-env-295.title: Iodine, the element missing from inland mountains
soil-env-295.text: About two billion people get too little iodine simply because of where their food grows. Iodine deficiency is a lack of this essential dietary trace element, which the thyroid hormones need. It is common in remote inland and especially mountainous areas. There, food grows in iodine-poor soil and nobody eats marine foods. The burden falls particularly on the Western Pacific, South-East Asia and Africa. The lack causes goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland, which affected 187 million people in 2010. In the womb it causes a syndrome of developmental delay, making it a preventable cause of intellectual disability. The main prevention is cheap. Adding small amounts of iodine to table salt costs only a few cents a ton. A shortage of selenium, described in {{ref:soil-env-296}}, is among its risk factors.

soil-env-296.title: Selenium: when the soil runs short, so does the body
soil-env-296.text: Finland adds selenium salts to its chemical fertilizers to raise the selenium in its soil. The reason is selenium deficiency: a shortage of this critical nutrient below the levels an organism requires. People who depend on food grown in selenium-deficient soil are at risk. Croplands and diets run low in regions of China, Europe, Russia and New Zealand. Climate change is predicted to strip selenium from croplands and make the shortage commoner. Combined with Coxsackievirus, it causes {{ref:soil-env-297}}. Together with a lack of iodine, it contributes to Kashin-Beck disease of cartilage. Livestock suffer too. In them it causes white muscle disease. Ruminants, the cud-chewing grazers, are especially prone because they absorb less selenium, particularly from forage. Recommended adult intake is 55 μg/day in the US and 70 μg/day from the European Food Safety Authority.

soil-env-294.title: Melioidosis, the soil bacterium called a time bomb
soil-env-294.text: Soldiers came home from Vietnam apparently healthy and fell ill years later. Those latent infections earned melioidosis the name 'Vietnam Time Bomb'. It is an infectious disease caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil-dwelling bacterium of the kind met in {{ref:soil-bio-002}}. People catch it by contact with contaminated soil or water. The bacterium is most abundant 10 to 90 cm deep in soil and also lives in ponds, streams and rice paddies. It is hardy. It survives more than 16 years in nutrient-poor settings such as desert soil, and tolerates pH 4.5 for 70 days. It enters the body through wounds, inhalation or ingestion. The disease is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and cases rise with heavy rain and storms. A 2016 model estimated about 165,000 infections and 89,000 deaths a year. Diabetes is a major risk factor. There is no approved vaccine, so prevention means protective gear and avoiding direct contact with soil and water.

soil-env-288.title: Geophagia, the ancient habit of eating earth
soil-env-288.text: Over 100 species of primates eat dirt on purpose. Geophagia is the deliberate eating of earth or earth-like substances such as clay, chalk or termite-mound soil, by animals and people. In primates it protects against parasites, supplies minerals and helps neutralize toxic compounds in leaves. The oldest evidence comes from Kalambo Falls, where calcium-rich white clay lay alongside the bones of Homo habilis. In people it is most often reported in children and pregnant women, and it is classed as a form of pica, the eating of things that are not food. {{ref:soil-chem-079}} may protect the stomach against toxins, parasites and pathogens, and many soils supply calcium, iron and zinc. In Cameroon markets kaolin is sold for eating, and pregnant women take it against nausea despite possibly dangerous levels of arsenic and lead. Soil has other risks. Faecally contaminated earth can pass on the eggs of parasitic worms such as Ascaris, which survive in soil for years, as well as tetanus and lead poisoning. The habit also has a commercial side. Bentonite and kaolin are sold as digestive aids, and attapulgite clay is an active ingredient in anti-diarrhoeal medicines.

soil-env-292.title: Roundworms in the soil, the commonest human parasites
soil-env-292.text: About two billion people carry worms picked up from soil, and four billion are at risk. Soil-transmitted helminthiasis is infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces. It takes three forms: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm. Together they make the most common human parasitic disease. The worms are nematodes, the animals of {{ref:soil-bio-193}}. Eggs passed in faeces mature into infective larvae in the soil, and people swallow them on unwashed produce or hands. Hookworm larvae work differently: they hatch and penetrate the skin. Open defecation, lack of hand washing and walking barefoot on contaminated soil are the main causes. So the disease is commonest in warm, moist, poorly sanitized regions. Hookworm affects an estimated 740 million people and is the leading cause of anaemia and protein deficiency in developing nations. Deworming reduces worm burdens, but reinfection follows continued exposure. Improved water, sanitation and hygiene lower the odds of infection.

soil-env-304.title: Prions, the infectious proteins that cling to clay
soil-env-304.text: A prion carries no DNA or RNA, yet it spreads disease. It is a misfolded protein that makes normal copies of the same protein misfold, causing fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative diseases. Scrapie, BSE, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and {{ref:soil-env-305}} are among them. Shed from carcasses and body fluids, prions may linger in soil by binding to clay and other minerals. Unbound prions degrade over time, but soil-bound ones stay stable or increase, so prions likely accumulate in the environment. Repeated wetting and drying may reduce their infectivity, depending on soil type. Hamsters fed grass grown where an infected deer was buried became ill, so plants can carry prions.

soil-env-297.title: Keshan disease, a heart illness written in the soil
soil-env-297.text: A belt of heart disease once ran from northeast to southwest China. Keshan disease is a congestive cardiomyopathy, a failing of the heart muscle, caused by dietary selenium deficiency together with a mutated strain of Coxsackievirus. It is named after Keshan County. Every case traced back to selenium-deficient soil, and the disease peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands. The shortage appears to let a more virulent viral strain dominate. Decades of selenium supplementation reduced it. Some patients use Astragalus, a herb that accumulates selenium from soil. Garlic, onions and broccoli are good selenium sources only if their soil contains it.

soil-env-303.title: One Health: people, animals and soil as one system
soil-env-303.text: Diseases that jump from animals to people, called zoonotic diseases, gave rise to One Health. It is an integrated approach that seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together. It grew from the awareness that human health, animal health and ecological change are interdependent. Antimicrobial resistance is treated as a One Health issue. Misuse of antimicrobials in medicine, veterinary care and farming selects resistant organisms, and wastewater, soil and runoff spread them. The FAO, WHO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and UNEP back the approach.

soil-env-291.title: Podoconiosis, red clay that swells the legs
soil-env-291.text: An estimated 4 million people have legs swollen by the soil they walk on, 1.5 million of them in Ethiopia. Podoconiosis, also called nonfilarial elephantiasis, is a disease of the lymphatic vessels of the lower legs, caused by long-term barefoot contact with irritant soils. After lymphatic filariasis, it is the second most common cause of tropical lymphoedema, a disfiguring swelling of the legs. It strikes genetically susceptible people on red clay soils formed over alkaline volcanic bedrock, in highlands with about 1500 mm of rain at 1500 m altitude. Soil particles penetrate the feet. Macrophages, immune cells that engulf foreign matter, take them up, and the particles collect in lymph nodes. Ernest Price found silicon, aluminium and other soil metals inside macrophages in patients' lymph nodes. The result is chronic inflammation, scarring and blockage. Affected areas are rich in kaolinite and gibbsite. Smectite, mica, quartz and iron oxides are also suspects, but no single culprit is proven. Wearing shoes and using floor coverings prevent it.

soil-env-305.title: Chronic wasting disease and the ground that spreads it
soil-env-305.text: For grazing deer, the ground itself may be the main danger. Chronic wasting disease is a fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy, a brain-wasting illness caused by prions. It naturally affects deer, elk, moose and their relatives. Infected animals shed prions, and other animals catch them by eating grass growing in contaminated soil. The prions stay infectious in the environment for years. They bind so tightly to soil particles that the soil may be a major route of transmission. Prions mixed with clay infected deer through the nose, and by 2006 they were shown to bind to sandy quartz clay minerals. After a Quebec outbreak, inspectors ordered 25 cm of soil decontaminated in parts of the farm.

soil-env-302.title: Mycobacterium vaccae, the soil microbe that calmed mice
soil-env-302.text: In Uganda, locals said a muddy substance could cure ailments. There, scientists first isolated Mycobacterium vaccae, a nonpathogenic bacterium, one that causes no disease, which lives naturally in soil. It belongs to the Mycobacteriaceae, and its name comes from cow dung, where the first strain was cultured. Heat-killed cells injected into mice raised serotonin and lowered anxiety. Mice fed live cells ran a maze twice as fast, with less anxiety. Vaccines made from killed cells are being studied for asthma, depression, psoriasis, eczema and tuberculosis.

soil-env-299.title: Replacing the poisoned paddies of the Jinzū River
soil-env-299.text: Cleaning up after {{ref:soil-env-298}} took decades. The cleanup of cadmium-polluted farmland along the Jinzū River followed the lawsuit over that disease. Japan's 1970 agricultural soil contamination law stopped planting for restoration wherever soil held 1 ppm cadmium or more. By 1977, 1,500 hectares had been designated. Topsoil replacement, one of the options in {{ref:soil-env-012}}, began in 1979. By 2012 it had covered 863 hectares at a cost of ¥40.7 billion. By 1996 cadmium in the farmland had returned to a background level of 0.1 ppb.

soil-env-289.title: Why parrots flock to eat one layer of clay
soil-env-289.text: On the Manu River, parrots eat from one specific soil layer and ignore the layers a metre above or below it. Avian geophagy is the eating of clay-rich soil by birds, notably South American parrots at clay licks. The preferred soils are rich in smectite, kaolin and mica and have far higher cation-exchange capacity. That lets them bind toxins from seeds, which become positively charged in the stomach. Yet the eaten soils are also consistently higher in sodium, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean. Sodium is likely the main driver.

soil-env-290.title: Cattle and sheep that eat soil with every bite
soil-env-290.text: Grazing animals swallow soil without meaning to. Soil ingestion by livestock happens when the hooves of cattle and sheep press soil onto pasture plants, which the animals then eat. It is measured from the ash content of their faeces. Intake is greatest on weak, poorly drained soils in wet autumn and winter conditions. The soil is not all harm. It supplies iron, manganese, zinc, cobalt, copper, selenium and iodine that herbage lacks. It can, however, wear down sheep's incisors.

soil-env-300.title: Biofortification: breeding nutrients into the crop itself
soil-env-300.text: In Mozambique, sweet potatoes rich in beta-carotene cut vitamin A deficiency in children by 24%. That is biofortification: breeding crops, conventionally or by genetic engineering, so that they contain more nutrients as they grow. It targets shortages of micronutrients such as vitamin A, zinc and iron in low- and middle-income countries. It reaches the rural poor, who rarely get fortified foods. In India, iron- and zinc-rich pearl millet improved iron status. Researchers are developing bread grain biofortified with selenium to raise low selenium levels in British grains. Critics warn it may simplify diets further and urge that it be part of wider food diversification.

soil-env-301.title: The hygiene hypothesis and the microbes that may tune immunity
soil-env-301.text: Most mammalian evolution took place in mud and rotting vegetation. The hygiene hypothesis asks what that history means for allergies. It is the idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system. In 2003 Graham Rook recast it as the 'old friends' hypothesis. His version focuses on microbes that co-evolved with humans, including ambient species sharing human environments, rather than recent crowd infections. The idea is not about personal cleanliness: poor hygiene raises infection risk without lowering allergy risk. The question is still open. Much evidence supports the hypothesis, yet many scientists reject it, and it struggles to explain allergies in less affluent regions.

openers.soils-and-human-health: Soil feeds people, and sometimes it poisons, infects or starves them. In Toyama Prefecture, Japan, a mass cadmium poisoning from about 1912 was named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused. Elsewhere people inhale fungal spores, catch bacteria and roundworms from contaminated ground, or sicken because their food grows without enough iodine or selenium. Some animals and people even eat earth on purpose. This chapter follows those links between the ground and health, and ends with an approach that tries to balance the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together.

reviews.soils-and-human-health: Soil reaches human health along several paths at once. It can poison, as cadmium did through the rice paddies of the Jinzū River, or starve, as iodine-poor and selenium-poor soils do from inland mountains to a belt across China. It harbors fungi, bacteria, roundworms and clay-bound prions, often stirred up by rain, drought, dust or bare feet. Yet animals and people also eat earth on purpose, and clay and soil microbes may protect the stomach or tune the immune system. Medical geology and One Health share one lesson: as Paracelsus put it, the dose makes the poison, and health depends on balance.
